title: At the Sign of the Golden Fleece: Prince Hall, African Lodge, and the Warrant Carried Across the Atlantic
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Massachusetts, the country he names as his own
stops.date_confidence: Birth year unresolved, four candidates. Death notices giving his age as 72 point to 1735, and the Massachusetts Historical Society renders his dates 1735-1807. A letter of Rev. Jeremy Belknap, 1795, gives a range, 1737 or 1738; the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Massachusetts adopted 1738 from it. A deposition of 31 August 1807 records his age as 'about 70 years', pointing to c. 1737. Grimshaw says 1748. The field carries 1735 and settles nothing. The coordinate is the centroid of Massachusetts, not of New England; Hall's own word is the wider one. This stop precedes the Bridgetown stop because 1735 is the earliest of the four candidate years, not because the atlas prefers it.
stops.campa: In his printed charges Hall names New England as his country, not Africa and not the islands. He never names a town. The pin is the geographic center of Massachusetts, which is what the record forces: a New England man by his own word, a man of no fixed birthplace by every other. James Sidbury reads him as native to the region. Four birth years compete in print, 1735 and 1737 and 1738 and 1748, each carrying a document behind it, and not one of those documents is a register of birth.
suggested_refs: Massachusetts Historical Society biographical dates for Prince Hall (1735-1807)
The Belknap letter of 1795, source of the 1737 or 1738 range
sources: James Sidbury, cited in Wikipedia, 'Prince Hall'

stops.name: Bridgetown, the birth Grimshaw asserts
stops.date_confidence: Contested tradition, [R]. William H. Grimshaw, Official History of Freemasonry Among the Colored People (1903), gives Bridgetown and about 1748. No primary document supports either. Later Masonic scholars, including Peter P. Hinks, treat Grimshaw as embellishing and in places fabricating. Month and day are given nowhere and default to 01.
stops.campa: Barbados enters the story through a book printed ninety-six years after Prince Hall dies. William Grimshaw gives the island a birth: a son of an Englishman and a free Black woman of French descent, born at Bridgetown, carried north as a boy. No baptism record and no ship's list has ever been produced for it, and Hall himself never writes the word Barbados in anything he signs. The Prince Hall Grand Lodge of the Caribbean, seated at Christ Church on this same island, keeps the tradition and cites it as fact. The pin marks where the claim puts him.
suggested_refs: Grimshaw, Official History of Freemasonry Among the Colored People of North America (1903), the sole source for Bridgetown
sources: William H. Grimshaw, Official History of Freemasonry Among the Colored People of North America (1903)
Wikipedia, 'Prince Hall Freemasonry' (Prince Hall Grand Lodge of the Caribbean tradition)

stops.name: Boston, the tanner's shop
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, [R]. Charles H. Wesley theorized enslavement from about age eleven to a Boston tanner named William Hall. The year here is arithmetic, Wesley's 'about eleven' laid against a late-1730s birth, not evidence. No Boston tax record, deed, or business directory reachable in this pass locates the tannery; the coordinate is central Boston, not the shop.
stops.campa: A Boston tanner named William Hall keeps a boy of about eleven, and the boy learns to dress and process leather in his shop. That is Charles Wesley's reconstruction. The shop's street has never been found in a tax list or a business record, and the trade shows up only downstream, in a state supply order for artillery drumheads and in a lodge that will meet at the sign of a fleece because the sign hangs over its founder's own workbench. The surname the man carries out of the shop is the tanner's.
suggested_refs: Charles H. Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977), chapter on the Boston years
sources: Charles H. Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977), cited in Wikipedia, 'Prince Hall'

stops.name: Boston, the household the records will not confirm
stops.date_confidence: Disputed, [R]. PBS's Africans in America and other secondary accounts give Hall a wife named Delia and a son, Primus, born 1756. David L. Gray found no records supporting the account, and the paternity of Primus Hall, who is independently documented, remains contested. The year is the year the claim asserts.
stops.campa: A wife named Delia and a son named Primus enter the record through secondary accounts, PBS among them, and leave it again when anyone looks for paper. David Gray searched and found nothing supporting the marriage. Primus Hall is a documented man in his own right, and the question of whose son he was stays open. The pin stands here because the claim is repeated often enough to need answering, and the year on it is the year the claim gives rather than a year any register gives.
suggested_refs: David L. Gray, Inside Prince Hall (2019), on the documentary silence around Delia and Primus
sources: David L. Gray, cited in Wikipedia, 'Prince Hall'

stops.name: Boston, joining a Congregational church
stops.date_confidence: Year attested in the biographical literature, [A]. Which congregation is not established; the coordinate is Boston's meetinghouse district, not an identified church. Gap stated rather than filled.
stops.campa: Prince Hall joins a Congregational church in Boston eight years before any document calls him free. Which congregation is not recorded. The step tells his biographers what the manumission paper does not. He is already resident and already known, moving inside the town's religious life while his legal condition remains whatever a Boston tanner says it is. Church membership in this town is a public standing. He takes it first, and the certificate follows eight years later.
suggested_refs: Massachusetts church membership records cited in Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977)
sources: Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977)

segments.name: A Free Man in a Slave Town

stops.name: Boston, the death of Sarah Ritchie
stops.date_confidence: Year attested, [A]. Nothing else about Sarah Ritchie, also recorded as Ritchery, survives in reachable sources: no age, no burial place, no words. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Sarah Ritchie, also written Ritchery, dies in Boston. She is Hall's first wife and she is enslaved, and beyond her name and her status the record holds nothing at all: no age, no burial place, no words of her own, no year of birth. Nothing further has surfaced to close the gap. Hall is somewhere in his thirties, a leatherworker in a harbor town where a great many households hold a person as property, and the paper that will call him a free man is still a year away.
suggested_refs: Prince Hall probate and vital records, Suffolk County, Massachusetts
sources: David L. Gray, Inside Prince Hall (2019), cited secondhand

stops.name: Boston, no longer reckoned a slave
stops.date_confidence: Certificate attested and dated, [A]; its corroboration is not. David L. Gray notes that no official Massachusetts record of a formal manumission has been located. The document's own text is the whole of the evidence, and it is quoted from Wesley's transcription rather than from the original.
stops.campa: A document dated the ninth of April declares Prince Hall no longer reckoned a slave but always accounted a free man. David Gray notes what is missing around it: no official Massachusetts record of the act of manumission has ever been located. The certificate speaks for itself and nothing speaks for the certificate. From this day the man in the leather shop signs petitions to a legislature and holds a warrant from London, and every institution he builds rests on one sheet of paper with no state file behind it.
stops.quote: no longer Reckoned a slave, but always accounted as a free man
stops.quote_source: Manumission certificate of Prince Hall, dated 9 April 1770, as transcribed in Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977)
suggested_refs: The 1770 manumission certificate, Boston; no corresponding Massachusetts state record located
sources: Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977)
David L. Gray, Inside Prince Hall (2019), cited secondhand

stops.name: Gloucester, the marriage to Flora Gibbs
stops.date_confidence: Year attested from Gloucester vital records, [A]; month and day are not recorded and default to 01. Because of that, whether the marriage precedes or follows the 9 April certificate is not established, and the stop order here is not an argument for either sequence.
stops.campa: Thirty miles up the coast, at Gloucester, Hall marries Flora Gibbs. Only the year survives, so whether he rides north as a free man carrying the April certificate or as a man still waiting for it cannot be settled, and no register closes the question. The Boston leatherworker is known well enough thirty miles from his own town to take a wife there, and the vital records of the fishing port enter his name without a qualifier attached to it. Sarah Ritchie has been dead a year.
suggested_refs: Gloucester, Massachusetts vital records for 1770
sources: Gloucester vital records cited in Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977)

segments.name: The Lodge That Would Not Have Him

stops.name: St. John's Lodge, the petition refused
stops.date_confidence: Event attested, [A]; date approximate. Sources place the refusal shortly before the March 1775 initiation without giving a day, so the field defaults to 01 January of that year. The lodge's meeting place in 1775 is not fixed by the sources used here.
stops.campa: Fifteen free Black men of Boston, Prince Hall among them, petition St. John's Lodge for admission to Freemasonry and are refused. The lodge is white, chartered under the English constitution, respectable, and it says no. Had it said yes there would be no African Lodge, no warrant from London, and no separate Grand Lodge system running two centuries on its own charter. Benjamin Franklin had been received by a St John's Lodge in Philadelphia forty-four years earlier without being asked twice.
suggested_refs: Prince Hall's own account of the refusal, in his letters to the African Lodge

stops.name: Boston, initiated by Lodge No. 441
stops.date_confidence: Date attested, [A]. The attribution to Sergeant John Batt comes through Wesley, [R]. The building used by this itinerant military lodge is not recorded anywhere reachable; the coordinate is central Boston, and the gap is handled as the corpus already handles Franklin's unfixed 1731 lodge room.
stops.campa: Refused by the town's own Masons, the fifteen are received by the army occupying the town. Lodge No. 441 of the Grand Lodge of Ireland travels with a British regiment garrisoned in Boston, and Sergeant John Batt initiates Prince Hall and his fourteen brethren into the craft. The building is not recorded and this stop does not invent one. Five weeks later the same army marches to Concord. Black Boston enters Freemasonry through a door held open by the empire it is about to fight.
suggested_refs: The 1775 permit granted by Lodge No. 441 to the newly initiated brethren
sources: Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977)

stops.name: Charlestown, six men of the same name
stops.date_confidence: Battle attested, [A]; Hall's presence is not, [R]. At least six men named Prince Hall served from Massachusetts per Massachusetts Soldiers and Sailors of the Revolutionary War (1896-1908), and no reachable source separates them. His biographers write that service is believed but not certain. Pinned as an unproven tradition.
stops.campa: On the heights above Charlestown the militia holds two assaults and loses the third, and Massachusetts muster rolls carry the name Prince Hall. So do five other rolls: at least six men of that name serve from the colony, and no reachable source separates them. Genealogists place him here; his biographers write that it is believed but not certain. A name repeated six times in one archive proves the name, and nothing about which of the six men holding it stood on this hill.
suggested_refs: Massachusetts Soldiers and Sailors of the Revolutionary War (1896-1908), the six Prince Hall entries
sources: Massachusetts Soldiers and Sailors of the Revolutionary War, cross-referenced in Wesley (1977)

stops.name: Cambridge, the army on the other side of the river
stops.date_confidence: Attested, [A], and inherited byte-identical from george_washington.journey.json, which places Washington's siege headquarters at the Vassall house from July 1775 to April 1776. The juxtaposition with African Lodge is the atlas's own; no source connects the two men.
stops.campa: Across the Charles, George Washington takes command of the army encircling Boston and keeps his headquarters in the Vassall house from July until the British sail out in March. The siege lines run for months within sight of the town where the fifteen Black Masons meet on a military permit issued by the besieged garrison. Two American institutions are being founded in the same few square miles, one by a Virginia slaveholder with a continental commission, one by a Boston leatherworker with no charter at all.
suggested_refs: The Vassall house, Cambridge, Washington's headquarters through the siege of Boston

stops.name: Boston, African Lodge No. 1
stops.date_confidence: Date attested, [A]. Note the naming order, which Wikipedia's 'Prince Hall' article reverses: the lodge is No. 1 first, on the 1775 permit, is chartered No. 459 in 1784, and reverts to No. 1 after declaring independence from the English register in 1827. Wikipedia's 'Prince Hall Freemasonry' article states the sequence correctly.
stops.campa: On the third of July, Prince Hall and his brethren constitute African Lodge No. 1. They have a permit from an Irish military lodge and nothing else: no charter, no grand lodge, no recognition from any body in America. They can bury their dead with Masonic rites and march on the feast of Saint John, and that is the whole of their authority. One day later, in Philadelphia, the Continental Congress declares a country independent. Neither body has yet been granted the standing it has just assumed.
suggested_refs: The African Lodge No. 1 founding permit of 1776
sources: Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977)

stops.name: The Massachusetts General Court, the petition against slavery
stops.date_confidence: Petition attested to 1777, [A], Massachusetts Archives; month and day not established here and default to 01. Hall is one signatory among several and the drafting hand is not identified.
stops.campa: Hall puts his name to a petition asking the Massachusetts legislature to abolish slavery in the state, arguing from the same premise the colony has just declared against London: that a people may not be held by a power they did not consent to. The house takes no action. This is the first of the petitions and it sets the method of all of them, which is to quote the Revolution back to itself in the plainest words available and to file the same argument again when the first one fails.
suggested_refs: Petition for the abolition of slavery, Massachusetts General Court, 1777, Massachusetts Archives

stops.name: Water Street, five drumheads for the artillery
stops.date_confidence: Month attested, [A], from Massachusetts state supply records; the day is not given and defaults to 01. The coordinate is Water Street, where the shop at the sign of the Golden Fleece stood, per the sources that place African Lodge's 1787 constitution there.
stops.campa: An artillery regiment of Boston orders five drumheads and Prince Hall makes them. The entry in the state supply records is a few lines long and it is the clearest surviving evidence of how he earns his living: hide, lime, scraper, stretched skin, a trade learned in a tanner's shop from about the age of eleven. The drums go to the war. The shop keeps its sign, a golden fleece, and within ten years the first chartered Black Masonic lodge in America will hold its meetings under it.
suggested_refs: Massachusetts state supply records, April 1777, the drumhead order
sources: Massachusetts state supply records cited in Wesley (1977)

stops.name: The Goose and Gridiron, the Grand Lodge constituted
stops.date_confidence: Attested, [A], and inherited byte-identical from hiram_abiff.journey.json. The stop runs before Hall's lifetime by design: it is the institutional origin of the warrant he petitions for in 1784. Its bearing on Prince Hall Freemasonry specifically is inference, [R], drawn from the shared ritual and charter machinery.
stops.campa: Sixty-seven years before the warrant, four London lodges meet at the Goose and Gridiron alehouse in St Paul's Churchyard and constitute themselves a Grand Lodge. Everything Prince Hall will petition for passes through this room: the degrees, the officers, the right to charter daughter lodges, and the legend of Hiram Abiff, the murdered builder of Solomon's temple, whose burial the third degree reenacts. The room predates every lodge that will ever stage that burial, Hall's included.
suggested_refs: The Goose and Gridiron alehouse, St Paul's Churchyard, site of the 1717 constitution

stops.name: Philadelphia, Franklin prints the Constitutions
stops.date_confidence: Attested, [A], and inherited byte-identical from benjamin_franklin.journey.json; that file also notes that no reachable source fixes the meeting place of Franklin's own 1731 initiation, a gap this journey reproduces for Hall's 1775 initiation. Month and day of the imprint default to 01.
stops.campa: Benjamin Franklin, initiated at St John's Lodge in this city three years before, sets the type for the first Masonic book printed in America: Anderson's Constitutions of the Free-Masons, reprinted from the London edition. The craft legend crosses the ocean as a Philadelphia imprint. Forty-one years later fifteen Black men in Boston are refused by a lodge of the same name Franklin joined, and take the same degrees from an Irish regimental lodge instead.
suggested_refs: Franklin's 1734 Philadelphia reprint of Anderson's Constitutions of the Free-Masons

stops.name: London, the Duke of Cumberland signs the warrant
stops.date_confidence: Date and issuing body attested, [A]. The warrant was issued in London by the Premier Grand Lodge of England under Grand Master H.R.H. the Duke of Cumberland; the research pool wrongly tagged this event to Boston, collapsing a three-year Atlantic transit into one pin. The coordinate is the Grand Lodge's Great Queen Street seat, not a documented signing room.
stops.campa: The Premier Grand Lodge of England, under the Grand Mastership of the Duke of Cumberland, signs a warrant chartering African Lodge as No. 459 on the register of England. Prince Hall never sees the room and never crosses the Atlantic. He has petitioned by letter, from a leather shop in Boston, a body that has just finished losing a war to his country, and it has answered him with the same instrument it grants to any lodge of Englishmen. The warrant now has to be carried three thousand miles.
suggested_refs: The warrant of 29 September 1784 to African Lodge No. 459, United Grand Lodge of England archives
sources: United Grand Lodge of England archives, cited secondhand

stops.name: Boston, Captain Scott brings the warrant ashore
stops.date_confidence: Attested, [A], in the Masonic historical literature: the warrant was carried to Boston by Captain James Scott and delivered to Hall personally on 29 April 1787. The delivery point is given as Hall himself rather than an address; the coordinate is the Water Street shop.
stops.campa: Captain James Scott brings the warrant ashore at Boston and puts it into Prince Hall's hands. Two years and seven months have passed since the Duke of Cumberland signed it; the Atlantic, not the Grand Lodge, is the delay. For the first time a lodge of Black Americans holds a document that any Mason in the English-speaking world is bound to acknowledge. Hall is somewhere near fifty and has waited twelve years since a Boston lodge told fifteen men they could not be admitted.
suggested_refs: Captain James Scott's delivery of the African Lodge warrant, 29 April 1787
sources: MasterMason.com, on the African Lodge warrant

stops.name: The Golden Fleece, African Lodge No. 459 constituted
stops.date_confidence: Date and place attested, [A]: constituted 6 May 1787 at the Golden Fleece on Water Street. The research pool described the Golden Fleece as a waterfront tavern at 42.3608, -71.0535 and separately listed 'Hall's leather shop' at 42.3601, -71.0589; the two entries describe one premises. Corrected to a single Water Street coordinate, approximate to the street rather than the doorway.
stops.campa: A week after the warrant lands, African Lodge No. 459 is formally constituted at the Golden Fleece on Water Street. The Golden Fleece is not a tavern. It is the sign over Prince Hall's own leather-dressing shop, and the first chartered Black Masonic lodge in America is therefore seated at its founder's workbench, among hides and lime and stretching frames. The officers are installed, the charter is read, and the lodge that began on a soldier's permit becomes a lodge on the register of England.
suggested_refs: The sign of the Golden Fleece, Water Street, Boston, Hall's shop and the lodge's meeting room
sources: Most Worshipful Union Grand Lodge of Florida

stops.name: The General Court, seventy-three names and a plan to return
stops.date_confidence: Year attested, [A], per PBS, 'Africans in America / The Boston Plan': a committee of twelve of the African Lodge headed by Hall, petition signed by seventy-three African Blacks. The research pool dated this January 1773 and tagged it attested; that is a Wikipedia error, doubly defective because it also names a Massachusetts Senate that did not exist until the 1780 constitution. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: A committee of twelve from African Lodge, headed by Prince Hall, brings the General Court a petition signed by seventy-three men who describe themselves as African Blacks. They ask for support to return to Africa, which they call their native country, and they set out a plan. Hall elsewhere calls New England his homeland; the two statements sit in the same decade, unreconciled. The court does not act. The number seventy-three is what dates the document.
suggested_refs: The 1787 emigration petition of seventy-three signers to the Massachusetts General Court
sources: PBS, 'Africans in America / The Boston Plan'

stops.name: The General Court, taxation without representation
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 1787, [A]. The research pool merged this school petition with the 1788 kidnapping petition under a single date; they are separate documents from separate years and are split here. Month and day not established, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The same committee of twelve petitions the General Court for schooling. Black Bostonians pay the taxes that fund the town's schools and their children are shut out of them, and Hall makes the argument the Revolution has just made famous, that taxation without representation is a grievance. The court declines. He petitions again and is declined again. The third attempt is not a petition: he opens a school in his own house and teaches the children himself. The address has not survived.
suggested_refs: Petition for a school for African children, Massachusetts General Court, 1787, Massachusetts Archives

stops.name: Boston, the school in his own house
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, [R], resting on Wesley at one remove. The school is well attested in the biographical tradition; its start date is not, and the house's address has not survived in any deed, tax list, or directory reachable here. The coordinate is central Boston and the year is indicative.
stops.campa: Twice refused public money, Hall runs the school out of his own rooms, teaching liberal arts and the classical subjects a Boston gentleman's son would be given. What he cannot get from the state he supplies from a leatherworker's income. The address is lost; no deed, tax list, or directory reachable now fixes the house. What is fixed is the sequence: petition, refusal, petition, refusal, and then a man in his fifties clearing a table and beginning without them.
suggested_refs: Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977), on the school in Hall's house
sources: Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977), cited secondhand

stops.name: The General Court, the kidnapping petition
stops.date_confidence: Date, text, and authorship attested, [A]. Printed in The American Museum vol. 3 (Carey, 1788) and preserved in manuscript at the Massachusetts Historical Society, item 670, in Hall's phonetic spelling. Citation flag: the pool gave pp. 410-411; the passage sits at scan pp. 414-415 of Internet Archive item americanmuseumor03care, so the printed folio should be checked before republication.
stops.campa: Three free Black Bostonians are lured aboard a vessel in the harbor on a pretence of distress, ironed, and carried off to be sold in the West Indies. Hall petitions the General Court on the twenty-seventh of February, naming the practice and demanding the state answer for men taken out of its own port. The petition is printed the same year in Philadelphia, in the American Museum, which carries the case out of Massachusetts and into the national press.
stops.quote: A captain under pretence that his vessel was in distress on an island below in this harbour, having got them on board put them in irons, and carried them off from their wives and children, to be sold for slaves.
stops.quote_source: Petition of Prince Hall and other free Black Bostonians to the Massachusetts General Court, 27 February 1788, as printed in The American Museum, or Universal Magazine, vol. 3 (Philadelphia: Mathew Carey, 1788)
suggested_refs: The American Museum, or Universal Magazine, vol. 3 (1788), printing of the February 1788 petition
Massachusetts Historical Society, Collections Online item 670, the manuscript
sources: The American Museum, or Universal Magazine, vol. 3 (Carey, 1788), Internet Archive americanmuseumor03care
Massachusetts Historical Society, Collections Online item 670

stops.name: The General Court, the seamen who stay at home
stops.date_confidence: Same document as the preceding stop, [A]. The research pool's version of this passage silently dropped the clause 'and some of them we have heard from'; the ellipsis and the clause are restored here from the printed American Museum text. The manuscript at MHS carries the same sentence in Hall's own spelling.
stops.campa: The same petition turns from the three men taken to the trade they came from. Boston's Black seamen are being sold out of ships they signed onto as crew, and the ones who know the work best are the ones who now stay ashore. Hall sets the consequence down as an economic fact rather than an outrage: skilled men idle in the streets because the sea is no longer survivable for them. The state that will not protect a sailor has, by that refusal, closed a trade.
stops.quote: many of our free blacks, that have entered on board vessels as seamen, have been sold for slaves; and some of them we have heard from ... hence it is that many of us, who are good seamen, are obliged to stay at home through fear, and one half of our time loiter about the streets, for want of employ.
stops.quote_source: Petition of Prince Hall to the Massachusetts General Court, 27 February 1788, as printed in The American Museum, or Universal Magazine, vol. 3 (Philadelphia: Mathew Carey, 1788)
suggested_refs: The seamen clause of the February 1788 petition, American Museum vol. 3, scan pp. 414-415
sources: The American Museum, or Universal Magazine, vol. 3 (Carey, 1788)
Massachusetts Historical Society, Collections Online item 670

stops.name: Boston, named Provincial Grand Master
stops.date_confidence: Year attested, [A]; month and day are not recorded and default to 01. The coordinate is the Water Street lodge room, which is where African Lodge is meeting in this period, not a separately documented installation site.
stops.campa: Prince Hall is named Provincial Grand Master. The title is the English system's own vocabulary for a man who governs lodges in a province on the Grand Lodge's behalf, and it converts a single chartered lodge into a jurisdiction that can plant others. He is now able to do for Philadelphia and Providence what the Irish regimental lodge did for him in 1775, and what St. John's Lodge of Boston refused to do. Within six years there will be lodges in three cities.
suggested_refs: African Lodge minute records, 1791, on Hall's appointment as Provincial Grand Master
sources: Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977), cited secondhand

stops.name: Charlestown, the Charge at Brother William Smith's hall
stops.date_confidence: Date and place attested from the pamphlet's own title page, [A], confirmed in catalog records at the American Antiquarian Society, University of Michigan, NYPL, and the Oxford Text Archive. The research pool placed this charge in Boston; Charlestown was a separate municipality until its annexation in 1874. Coordinate approximate to Charlestown, since Brother William Smith's hall is not located.
stops.campa: Across the river at Charlestown, in the hall of Brother William Smith, Hall delivers a charge to the brethren on the feast of Saint John the Baptist and then has it printed. It is among the earliest surviving pieces of published political writing by a Black American. He speaks on the abolition of slavery in Massachusetts, on the duty of a Mason to a Mason, and on charity to all mankind as the mark and image of God. The pamphlet goes out under his name and his title.
stops.quote: Dearly and well beloved Brethren of the African Lodge, as through the goodness and mercy of God, we are once more met together, in order to celebrate the Festival of St. John the Baptist
stops.quote_source: Prince Hall, A Charge Delivered to the Brethren of the African Lodge on the 25th of June, 1792, at the Hall of Brother William Smith, in Charlestown (Boston, 1792), opening salutation
suggested_refs: The 1792 Charge, printed pamphlet, Evans-TCP N18755
sources: Evans-TCP N18755, Oxford Text Creation Partnership transcription
Catalog records, American Antiquarian Society, University of Michigan, NYPL, Oxford Text Archive

stops.name: Charlestown, Aethiopia stretching forth her hands
stops.date_confidence: Text attested, [A], from the 1792 pamphlet. The line as it circulates, 'Ethiopia shall stretch forth her hands', is not the pamphlet's reading: Hall writes Aethiopia and ends the clause 'unto me'. It is his own rendering, not KJV Psalm 68:31, and is frequently confused with the different 1797 line that uses the singular hand.
stops.campa: Midway through the charge Hall quotes scripture and rewrites it in the quoting. The line he gives is not the King James rendering; his Aethiopia stretches her hands unto me, and the speaker is the great Architect of the universal world. Five years on, in another town, he will use the figure again in the singular and attach it to the present tense: Ethiopia beginning to stretch forth her hand, out of a sink of slavery toward freedom and equality. The verse is the same. The tense is the argument.
stops.quote: Hear what the great Architect of the universal world saith, Aethiopia shall stretch forth her hands unto me.
stops.quote_source: Prince Hall, A Charge Delivered to the Brethren of the African Lodge on the 25th of June, 1792, in Charlestown (Boston, 1792)
suggested_refs: Evans-TCP N18755, the 1792 Charge, for the Aethiopia passage
sources: Evans-TCP N18755, Oxford Text Creation Partnership transcription

stops.name: Philadelphia, a lodge under Hall's warrant
stops.date_confidence: Date attested, [A]. The meeting hall is not identified in any surviving account, so the coordinate is the corpus's canonical Philadelphia pin, inherited byte-identical from benjamin_franklin.journey.json in preference to the research pool's 39.9496, -75.1503.
stops.campa: Hall travels to Philadelphia and organizes a lodge there under his own warrant, the first daughter of African Lodge. Benjamin Franklin has been dead seven years, and the St John's Lodge of this city that received Franklin in 1731 has no part in the founding. The meeting hall is not identified in any surviving account. Philadelphia holds the largest free Black community in the country, and Black Freemasonry now exists in two cities, its authority running from a Boston leather shop.
suggested_refs: African Lodge charter records for the Philadelphia lodge, 22 March 1797
sources: Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977), cited secondhand

stops.name: Menotomy, five years since the last charge
stops.date_confidence: Date and place attested from the pamphlet's own title page, [A]: 'A Charge, delivered to the African Lodge, June 24, 1797, at Menotomy.' The research pool placed this charge in Boston, about ten kilometres southeast. Menotomy is present-day Arlington; the coordinate is the town, not an identified hall.
stops.campa: Ten kilometres northwest of Boston, at Menotomy, Hall delivers his second published charge on the feast of Saint John. He opens by counting the interval since Charlestown. Menotomy is the village that will later be called Arlington, and in 1775 its militia bled the British column on its road back from Concord. The audience is the same lodge, the printer will be the same city, and the country town is far enough from the harbor that a man can say plainly what happens in the streets he has come from.
stops.quote: 'Tis now five years since I deliver'd a Charge to you on some parts and points of Masonry.
stops.quote_source: Prince Hall, A Charge Delivered to the African Lodge, June 24, 1797, at Menotomy (Boston, 1797), opening line
suggested_refs: The 1797 Menotomy Charge, printed pamphlet, Internet Archive item tract-c-74-charge-delivered-african-lodge
sources: Open Anthology of Earlier American Literature

stops.name: Menotomy, patience and the streets of Boston
stops.date_confidence: Text attested, [A], from the 1797 pamphlet scan. The version in wide circulation, including on Wikipedia, converts this passage to the first person ('we could not bear up under the daily insults we meet with'); the pamphlet is in the second person throughout. The pamphlet reading is quoted here and the modernized text is flagged, not used.
stops.campa: The charge turns to what the brethren meet with daily, and Hall addresses it in the second person, to their faces. He tells them that patience is not meekness but the only thing holding under insult, that they are shamefully abused on public days of recreation, that they may truly be said to carry their lives in their hands. He is describing Boston from ten kilometres outside it. The circulating modern text of this passage moves it into the first person; the pamphlet does not.
stops.quote: Patience I say, for were we not possess'd of a great measure of it you could not bear up under the daily insults you meet with in the streets of Boston; much more on public days of recreation, how are you shamefully abus'd, and that at such a degree, that you may truly be said to carry your lives in your hands
stops.quote_source: Prince Hall, A Charge Delivered to the African Lodge, June 24, 1797, at Menotomy (Boston, 1797)
suggested_refs: Internet Archive scan of the 1797 Menotomy pamphlet, for the second-person reading

stops.name: Menotomy, the dark day in the French West Indies
stops.date_confidence: Text attested, [A], from the 1797 pamphlet; the reference is to the 1791 uprising in Saint-Domingue, six years before the charge. Independently confirmed in the excerpt cited by Wikipedia and in the anthology transcription.
stops.campa: Hall asks the lodge to remember a dark day six years gone in the French West Indies, when nothing but the snap of the whip was heard from morning to evening, and then to look at what the enslaved of that colony have since done to their masters. Toussaint's generals hold Saint-Domingue while he speaks. He names the revolution in a Massachusetts meeting hall in the year John Adams takes office, and offers it to his brethren not as a warning but as evidence.
stops.quote: My brethren, let us remember what a dark day it was with our African brethren six years ago, in the French West Indies.
stops.quote_source: Prince Hall, A Charge Delivered to the African Lodge, June 24, 1797, at Menotomy (Boston, 1797)
suggested_refs: The Haitian Revolution passage of the 1797 Charge
sources: Open Anthology of Earlier American Literature

stops.name: Menotomy, the mob and the men who will not answer it
stops.date_confidence: Text attested, [A], from the 1797 pamphlet as transcribed in the Open Anthology of Earlier American Literature and confirmed against the Internet Archive scan. Part of the same passage as the patience lines; the pamphlet gives no incident, date, or place for the attacks it describes, so the reference is general rather than to a documented riot.
stops.campa: Hall tells the lodge why the crowds come in numbers. It is not courage on their side, he says, since they will not face a man singly, and it is not cowardice on his brethren's, since they choose to suffer wrong rather than do wrong and hand the town a disturbance to hang on them. The calculation is exact and it is made out loud, in a printed pamphlet, by a man who has spent twenty years asking a legislature for things and being refused each time he asks.
stops.quote: 'tis not for want of courage in you, for they know that they dare not face you man for man, but in a mob, which we despise, and had rather suffer wrong than to do wrong, to the disturbance of the community and the disgrace of our reputation
stops.quote_source: Prince Hall, A Charge Delivered to the African Lodge, June 24, 1797, at Menotomy (Boston, 1797)
suggested_refs: The mob passage of the 1797 Menotomy Charge
sources: Open Anthology of Earlier American Literature

stops.name: Providence, Hiram Lodge
stops.date_confidence: Date attested, [A]; the building is not recorded, so the coordinate is central Providence. The lodge is later known as Hiram Lodge No. 3. The day after the Menotomy charge is a tight itinerary and the sources do not describe the journey.
stops.campa: The day after Menotomy, Hall organizes a lodge at Providence that will be known as Hiram Lodge No. 3. Three cities now, in three states, chartered from a single warrant carried across the Atlantic by a sea captain ten years earlier. The building is not recorded. The name the Providence brethren choose is the murdered builder of the temple, the figure whose burial every one of these lodges reenacts and whose legend arrived in America as a Philadelphia reprint.
suggested_refs: Hiram Lodge No. 3 charter records, Providence, 25 June 1797
sources: Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977), cited secondhand

stops.name: Boston, the Kirby Street room
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, [R]. The Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Massachusetts holds that African Lodge later met in a room on Kirby Street; neither the date of the move nor the exact site is established in surviving lodge minutes. The year and the coordinate are both indicative and are flagged as such.
stops.campa: Tradition held by the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Massachusetts places the lodge, in Hall's last years, in a room on Kirby Street. Neither the date of the move nor the exact site survives in the minutes, and this pin is approximate by admission. The lodge has outgrown the shop. It is no longer fifteen men with a soldier's permit meeting under a leather sign but a body with daughter lodges in two other states, and it takes a room of its own. Hall is past sixty and still Grand Master.
suggested_refs: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Massachusetts historical tradition regarding the Kirby Street room
sources: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Massachusetts historical tradition, site and date unconfirmed

stops.name: Charleston, the Southern Jurisdiction constitutes itself
stops.date_confidence: Attested, [A], and inherited byte-identical from hiram_abiff.journey.json. The connection to Prince Hall is temporal overlap only, [R]: no institutional contact between the Supreme Council at Charleston and African Lodge is attested, and the later non-recognition is inference from the segregated history of the two systems.
stops.campa: At Charleston the Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite constitutes itself, the first body of the jurisdiction that will run the southern half of the country's Freemasonry. Prince Hall is alive, six years from death, holding a warrant from London and governing three lodges. The two systems never touch. Seventy years on, from this jurisdiction's seat, Albert Pike will rewrite the Hiram legend as comparative religion, and his rite will not recognize the lodges Hall chartered.
suggested_refs: The 1801 constitution of the Supreme Council, Scottish Rite Southern Jurisdiction, Charleston

stops.name: Boston, the death of Prince Hall
stops.date_confidence: Date attested, [A], from the death record and the biographical literature. His age at death is not: a deposition of 31 August 1807 says about 70 years, death notices say 72, and the four competing birth years give four answers. The house he died in is not identified; the coordinate is central Boston.
stops.campa: Prince Hall dies in Boston on the fourth of December, somewhere near seventy years old by the deposition taken that summer, seventy-two by the death notices, and any of four ages by the sources that disagree about his birth. He has been a Mason for thirty-two years and a Grand Master for sixteen. The institution he leaves behind is the oldest continuously operating organization founded by Black Americans, and it has never been recognized by the lodge that refused him in 1775.
suggested_refs: Boston death notices of December 1807 and the deposition of 31 August 1807

stops.name: Copp's Hill Burying Ground, the burial
stops.date_confidence: Burial at Copp's Hill attested, [A]; the 7 December date is inference from contemporary newspaper reports that Hall died on the 4th and was buried three days later, [R]. The 1835 stone reads 'Died Dec. 7', which on this reading records the funeral rather than the death. Stated as the likely explanation, not as proof. Coordinate from the burying ground's own record, 42.367322, -71.055844.
stops.campa: Three days after his death he is buried at Copp's Hill in the North End, among the colonial dead of the town he lived in for more than half a century. The stone that will be raised here gives the seventh of December as the day he died. The death record gives the fourth. Contemporary newspapers report a burial three days after the death, which means the stone almost certainly carries the day of the funeral rather than the day he died, a distinction later readers of the grave have not always made.
suggested_refs: Copp's Hill Burying Ground interment records, City of Boston
sources: Copp's Hill Burying Ground interment records

stops.name: Boston, an estate of forty-seven dollars and twenty-two cents
stops.date_confidence: Inventory attested, [A], Suffolk County probate: $47.22, no real property, Sylvia Ward Hall as executrix. The exact date of the probate is not given in reachable sources and defaults to 01 January 1808. Whether Sylvia, also recorded as Zilpha, is a later wife or the same person under a variant name is contested and left contested.
stops.campa: The probate of the estate returns forty-seven dollars and twenty-two cents and no real property. Sylvia Ward Hall, named in some records as Zilpha, administers it as executrix. The founder of a national institution, a Provincial Grand Master, correspondent of the Grand Lodge of England, dies owning a leatherworker's tools and not the room they sit in. The sequence of his marriages, Sarah Ritchie then Flora Gibbs then Sylvia, is disputed among researchers; the inventory is not.
suggested_refs: Prince Hall probate records, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, 1807-1808
sources: David L. Gray, Inside Prince Hall (2019), cited secondhand

stops.name: Boston, the African Grand Lodge
stops.date_confidence: Date attested, [A], from the African Grand Lodge founding minutes as cited in Wesley. The meeting place is not separately documented; the coordinate is the Water Street room African Lodge had been using. The 1827 declaration of independence and the reversion to No. 1 are attested separately.
stops.campa: Six months after his death the brethren of Boston, Philadelphia and Providence meet and organize the African Grand Lodge, uniting the three lodges he chartered into one governing body. It is the first grand lodge of Black Freemasonry in the country and it takes his authority as its own. In 1827 it will declare itself independent of the Grand Lodge of England and the Boston lodge will take back its first number, No. 1, the one it carried on a soldier's permit in 1776.
suggested_refs: African Grand Lodge founding minutes, 24 June 1808
sources: Wesley, Prince Hall: Life and Legacy (1977), cited secondhand

stops.name: Copp's Hill, the monument of 1835
stops.date_confidence: Date and inscription attested verbatim, [A]. The stone's 'Died Dec. 7, 1807' conflicts with the death record's 4 December; see the burial stop for the newspaper evidence that the stone carries the funeral date. Coordinate as for the burial; the research pool's afterlife lens gave 42.3656, -71.0552, some 200 m south, and is not followed.
stops.campa: Twenty-eight years after the burial the Masons raise a monument over the grave at Copp's Hill. The inscription names him first Grand Master of the colored Grand Lodge in Massachusetts and gives his death as the seventh of December, three days late, the funeral written into the stone as the death. By now the lodges he founded have declared their independence and taken his name; within a generation the whole system will be called Prince Hall Freemasonry.
stops.quote: Here lies ye body of Prince Hall, first Grand Master of the colored Grand Lodge in Mass. Died Dec. 7, 1807.
stops.quote_source: Inscription, Prince Hall memorial monument, Copp's Hill Burying Ground, Boston, dedicated 24 June 1835
suggested_refs: The 1835 memorial monument at Copp's Hill and its inscription
sources: Monument inscription, Copp's Hill Burying Ground

stops.name: Washington, the House of the Temple
stops.date_confidence: Pike's Morals and Dogma and the reading lineage running on to Rene Guenon and Theodor Reuss are attested per hiram_abiff.journey.json, [A], and the coordinate is inherited byte-identical from that file. The bearing on Prince Hall Freemasonry, including Pike's rite's non-recognition, is inference, [R], not stated in the corpus file. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: From the House of the Temple in Washington, Albert Pike publishes Morals and Dogma and reads Hiram Abiff out of the lodge and into comparative religion, a solar myth with Egyptian and Persian relatives. Rene Guenon and Theodor Reuss will both read him. None of them writes about the lodges Prince Hall chartered, and Pike's own rite does not recognize them. The legend travels upward into universal tradition while the men who reenact it in Boston are refused a handshake.
suggested_refs: Albert Pike, Morals and Dogma of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite (1871)

stops.name: Cambridge Common, the Clausen monument
stops.date_confidence: Unveiled May 2010, [A], per Wikipedia, 'Prince Hall Monument'; the day within the month is not given and defaults to 01. Coordinate from the monument's own listing, 42 degrees 22 minutes 34.9 seconds north by 71 degrees 07 minutes 16.5 seconds west. The research pool dated the dedication 1998 in one lens and called it unconfirmed in another, and its coordinate was in fact the corpus's canonical Cambridge pin, borrowed by accident.
stops.campa: Ted Clausen's monument to Prince Hall is unveiled on Cambridge Common, beside the Washington Elm and the Revolutionary War cannons, a few hundred metres from where George Washington kept his headquarters through the siege. Two hundred and thirty-five years after fifteen men were refused by a Boston lodge, the city puts one of them on the ground where the Continental Army camped. The date circulates wrongly as 1998 in several sources; the unveiling is in May 2010.
suggested_refs: Ted Clausen, Prince Hall Monument, Cambridge Common, unveiled May 2010

stops.name: Boston, forty-seven Grand Lodges of fifty-one
stops.date_confidence: Current as of this survey, [A], per Wikipedia, 'Prince Hall Freemasonry': 47 of 51 mainstream U.S. Grand Lodges recognize Prince Hall Grand Lodges as regular, with Mississippi, Louisiana, South Carolina and West Virginia outstanding. The date field carries the survey year; the figure changes as jurisdictions vote.
stops.campa: Forty-seven of the fifty-one mainstream American Grand Lodges now recognize Prince Hall Grand Lodges as regular. Mississippi, Louisiana, South Carolina and West Virginia do not. The refusal that began at St. John's Lodge in Boston in 1775 is therefore not a closed historical episode but a live jurisdictional fact in four states. Danielle Allen writes in 2021 of a forgotten Black founding father, which is a description of the reading, not of the man.
suggested_refs: Danielle Allen, 'A Forgotten Black Founding Father', The Atlantic (2021)

stops.name: Christ Church, the bust at Graeme Hall
stops.date_confidence: Existence attested, [A]; the year of erection is not, and no reachable source gives one, so the date field carries the survey year rather than the casting. Location corrected: the bust stands at the Prince Hall Masonic Centre, Graeme Hall, Christ Church, not at the research pool's 13.1939, -59.5432, which falls some fourteen kilometres inland in the uplands.
stops.campa: At Graeme Hall in Christ Church, Barbados, a bust of Prince Hall stands outside the Prince Hall Masonic Centre, on the island Grimshaw named as his birthplace in 1903 and no document has confirmed since. The Grand Lodge of the Caribbean seated here holds the tradition as its own origin. No reachable source gives the year the bust was raised, so the date on this stop is the year of the survey, not of the casting. Grimshaw's book is the whole of the evidence for the island, and the bust stands on it.
suggested_refs: The Prince Hall bust at the Prince Hall Masonic Centre, Graeme Hall, Christ Church, Barbados
